speakers.name: John Ternus
speakers.title: Incoming CEO (transitioning into the role in September)

exchanges.question: Procedural only: the host gave operator instructions and asked for the first question. No analyst question in this exchange.
exchanges.answer: None; procedural exchange with no question asked or answered.

exchanges.question: How much did demand outpace supply for iPhone and Mac in the March quarter, and does the June quarter guidance reflect supply constraints for those segments or is it an unconstrained guide? Follow-up to Kevan: expand on no longer providing net cash neutral as a formal target; does it imply a different capital return policy, and are the investments referenced organic or inorganic?
exchanges.answer: Tim: Apple was constrained in the March quarter primarily on iPhone and to a lesser extent on Mac, driven primarily by the availability of the advanced nodes its SoCs are produced on; in the June quarter the majority of constraints will be on several Mac models given continued high demand and less flexibility in the supply chain than normal. Two factors drive the Mac constraint: customer recognition of Mac Mini and Mac Studio as platforms for AI and agentic tools is happening faster than predicted, and customer response to MacBook Neo has been off the charts with higher-than-expected demand (helping set a March quarter record for customers new to Mac); the Mini and Mac Studio may take several months to reach supply-demand balance. He did not quantify how far demand exceeded supply. Kevan: net cash neutral has been a valuable framework since 2018, but Apple is now evaluating cash and debt independently to make more optimal economic decisions while remaining disciplined; it remains very committed to returning excess cash after investing in the business first, has returned over $1 trillion since the program started (over $850 billion via repurchases), and increased the buyback authorization by another $100 billion on top of leftover capacity from the prior authorization; the organic versus inorganic question was not addressed.

exchanges.question: How should investors think about the rise of AI agents and talk of an agentic smartphone: does it mean new products in a totally new form factor or change the game? Follow-up: how will margins trend after the June quarter given component costs and constraints; is 47%-48% a range Apple can stay in, or is there no visibility beyond June?
exchanges.answer: Tim declined to discuss the future road map, saying only that Apple is thrilled with iPhone growing 22% in the quarter after an incredible Q1, the strongest cycle in its history from launch through the March quarter. On margins he addressed memory specifically: the December quarter had a minimal memory impact; the March quarter saw higher memory costs partially offset by carry-in inventory; the June quarter guidance embeds significantly higher memory costs, also partly offset by carry-in inventory. Apple does not give color beyond June, but beyond the June quarter it believes memory costs will drive an increasing impact on the business; it will continue to evaluate and look at a range of options. He did not address whether 47%-48% is a sustainable range.

exchanges.question: How has MacBook Neo driven penetration with new customer segments such as education, value and emerging markets, how does Apple view underpenetrated markets more broadly, and how will the product road map inform that strategy? Follow-up: has the new App Store ad inventory been a notable contributor to services growth and outperformance, and what is the broader ad strategy given plans to introduce ads to Maps this summer?
exchanges.answer: Tim: Apple is currently supply constrained on MacBook Neo; it was very bullish before announcing it but undercalled the level of enthusiasm. The product is focused on bringing Mac to more people, especially customers new to Mac and those holding on to a Mac for a very long time, and both are doing well; school systems like Kansas City Public Schools are switching from Chromebooks and Windows PCs to MacBook Neo, with more such stories at the school system and individual consumer level. Kevan: advertising grew year-over-year; Apple recently introduced additional ads across App Store search results, and this summer in the U.S. and Canada Apple Maps will feature ads during key search and discovery moments for local businesses; Apple believes it can help businesses of all sizes grow via advertising while delivering a great customer experience and respecting privacy. He did not say whether the new ad inventory was a notable contributor.

exchanges.question: With memory costs rising beyond June, will Apple strategically prioritise share gain (e.g. not raising prices at the lower end where competitors struggle) or profitability, and what framework should investors use? Follow-up: in an agentic AI world, which parts of the stack will Apple build internally versus with partners, where will it invest more heavily over the next several years, and is that related to the net cash comments and building more infrastructure?
exchanges.answer: Tim: Apple will look at a range of options with memory costs increasing and he did not want to go beyond that at this point. On investment: Apple is clearly investing more, visible in OpEx, and R&D is accelerating much faster than the company as a whole; it is investing in both products and services and sees opportunities in both. Kevan: AI is a really important investment area and Apple is investing incrementally on top of what it normally invests in its product road map. Neither addressed the internal-versus-partner split or the link to the net cash change.

exchanges.question: What levers are driving 20%-plus iPhone growth for several quarters despite supply constraints, and how durable is that growth? Follow-up: what advice is Tim giving John Ternus to build on Apple's strengths while shaping the next chapter?
exchanges.answer: Tim: the iPhone 17 family is driving growth despite constraints, with customers loving the design, performance, durability, camera, Center Stage and integrated Apple Intelligence; growth is double digits in the majority of markets tracked (U.S., Latin America, Greater China, Western Europe, India, Japan, Southeast Asia), with a new March quarter record for upgraders and U.S. customer satisfaction of 99% for the 17 family. Durability of the growth was not addressed directly. On the transition: Steve Jobs' advice lifted a huge burden for him; his advice to John is that one of the most important decisions is where to spend his time, which should be where the greatest benefit to the company and users lies, and never to forget the North Star of making the best products that enrich people's lives.

exchanges.question: Is iPhone constrained in the June quarter, how is Apple securing both SoC and memory supply, is it considering alternative memory sources beyond traditional partners, and what drives confidence that iPhone is not constrained given share gains? Follow-up: are services gross margins approaching an asymptote given mix, or is there still volume leverage and lower losses in some categories to keep scaling margin?
exchanges.answer: Tim: the primary constraint in both the March and June quarters is the availability of the advanced nodes the SoCs are produced on, not memory; he will not predict when supply and demand match, believes Mac Mini and Mac Studio will take several months to reach balance, and Apple is not saying this ends anytime soon; it is not a problem per se, Apple simply undercalled demand and lead times take a while to correct. The majority of the June quarter constraint will be on Mac: Mac Mini, Mac Studio and MacBook Neo. Alternative memory sourcing was not addressed. Kevan: the services portfolio spans businesses with different models, profitability profiles and growth rates, so relative performance affects margin at any time; Q2 services margin rose 20 basis points sequentially, primarily on mix; it is hard to speculate how it evolves, though some services are improving in profitability as they gain scale and Apple is encouraged by the trajectory.

exchanges.question: Update on the two-pronged Apple foundational models strategy (collaboration with Google plus internal models): how is Apple balancing the two, and does it need to invest more to pursue both? Follow-up to Kevan: why was the sequential product gross margin moderation more muted than in recent years (mix, FX tailwind?), and what was the FX impact on gross margin for the quarter?
exchanges.answer: Tim: Apple is investing more, visible in OpEx, with R&D scaled rather significantly year-over-year; the collaboration with Google is going well and Apple is happy with its independent work too. Kevan: products gross margin decreased 200 basis points sequentially on a seasonal loss of leverage and higher memory costs; total company gross margin rose 110 basis points sequentially on favorable mix and lower tariff-related costs, partly offset by seasonal loss of leverage and higher memory costs. Tim: the 49.3% March quarter gross margin included tariff-related costs, which were lower than in December because of lower sequential product volume plus the full-quarter benefit of reduced IEEPA tariff rates and the reduced global tariff rate under Section 122; Apple is following established processes to apply for refunds of tariffs paid and plans to reinvest any amount received into U.S. innovation and advanced manufacturing as new investments in addition to prior U.S. commitments. Kevan: there was no sequential FX impact on gross margin from Q1 to Q2.

exchanges.question: What is Apple seeing in China, and is it gaining competitive advantage from supply constraints hitting competitors? Follow-up: how is the India market evolving in terms of the iPhone base, the rising middle class and the overall opportunity?
exchanges.answer: Tim: Greater China revenue grew 33% in the first half and 28% in the March quarter, a quarterly revenue record, driven by iPhone (also a March quarter record); iPhone was the top-selling model in urban China, Mac Mini the top-selling desktop and MacBook Air the top-selling laptop, and store traffic grew double digits during his March visit for the 50th anniversary. The competitor supply constraint angle was not addressed. India is a huge opportunity: the second-largest smartphone market and third-largest PC market where Apple still has a modest share, with many people moving into the middle class and the majority of customers across iPhone, Mac, iPad and Watch new to the product; he is over the moon excited about India.
